\chapter{Family and Friends}
\label{ch:ka-family-and-friends}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my family as a group in Kannada and name a friend, and say which of the two words is native and which is a Sanskrit loan.}

Say \kn{ಇದು} \kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಕುಟುಂಬ} and \kn{ಇವನು} \kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ}, trace kuṭumba and snēhita back to Sanskrit, and set snēhita beside the native pair \kn{ಗೆಳೆಯ}/\kn{ಗೆಳತಿ}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kuṭumba]{\kn{ಕುಟುಂಬ} (kuṭumba) — \textquotedblleft{}family,\textquotedblright{} the word the household words never needed}

\label{lesson:KA-C35-kutumba}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Nanage kannaḍa iṣṭa} closed the last chapter on a sentence built from nothing but nouns. This chapter opens on the plainest nouns of all: the words for the people you would actually say that sentence to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕುಟುಂಬ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಕುಟುಂಬ}} — \emph{kuṭumba} — \textbf{family}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಇದು} \kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಕುಟುಂಬ}.} — \emph{idu nanna kuṭumba.} — \textquotedblleft{}This is my family.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Nanna}, \textquotedblleft{}my,\textquotedblright{} has been yours since Chapter 2.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಕುಟುಂಬ}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{कुटुम्ब}} (\emph{kuṭumba}), \textquotedblleft{}family, household,\textquotedblright{} carried into Kannada whole — the same kind of loan as \textbf{\kn{ಇಷ್ಟ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಸಹಾಯ}}.

Chapter 12 gave you six words: \textbf{\kn{ಅಪ್ಪ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಅಮ್ಮ}}, and the four age-graded siblings \textbf{\kn{ಅಣ್ಣ}/\kn{ತಮ್ಮ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಅಕ್ಕ}/\kn{ತಂಗಿ}}. Every one is native Dravidian, and not one of them means \textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{} — each names a single specific person. Kannada never inherited a word for the group itself, so when it needed one, it reached for Sanskrit. The people came first, and stayed native; the collective came later, and came borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}idu nanna kuṭumba\textquotedblright{} — this is my family
  \item the six named people, then the borrowed group word — \textquotedblleft{}appa, amma, aṇṇa, tamma, akka, tangi … kuṭumba\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nanage kannaḍa iṣṭa\textquotedblright{} — once more, no verb in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}this is my family.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Idu nanna kuṭumba}.) Is \emph{kuṭumba} native Dravidian or a loan? (\textbf{A Sanskrit loan}, like \emph{iṣṭa} and \emph{sahāya}.) Name Chapter 12's six family words. (\emph{Appa, amma, aṇṇa, tamma, akka, tangi}.) Which of those six means \textquotedblleft{}family\textquotedblright{} as a group? (\textbf{None of them} — that's exactly the gap \emph{kuṭumba} fills.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[snēhita]{\kn{ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ} (snēhita) — \textquotedblleft{}friend,\textquotedblright{} built out of the word for oil}

\label{lesson:KA-C35-snehita}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kuṭumba} named the people you are born into. Not every important person in your life is one of them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ}} — \emph{snēhita} — \textbf{friend} (a woman friend is \textbf{\kn{ಸ್ನೇಹಿತೆ}}, \emph{snēhite})
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\kn{ಇವನು} \kn{ನನ್ನ} \kn{ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ}.} — \emph{ivanu nanna snēhita.} — \textquotedblleft{}He is my friend.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{स्नेहित}} (\emph{snēhita}), built on \textbf{\dv{स्नेह}} (\emph{snēha}). \emph{Snēha}'s \textbf{first} meaning is not \textquotedblleft{}affection\textquotedblright{} at all — it is \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}oil, unctuousness, smoothness.\textquotedblright{}} Only from there did it stretch to \textquotedblleft{}fondness, love\textquotedblright{}: a substance that makes things slide smoothly together became the word for whatever binds two people the same way.

Kannada also holds an inherited word for the same idea, and it did not retire when the Sanskrit one arrived: \textbf{\kn{ಗೆಳೆಯ}} (\emph{geḷeya}, a male friend) and \textbf{\kn{ಗೆಳತಿ}} (\emph{geḷati}, a female friend) are ordinary, everyday Dravidian words, sitting right beside \emph{snēhita} the way \textbf{\kn{ನೆರವು}} sits beside \emph{sahāya}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ivanu nanna snēhita\textquotedblright{} — he is my friend
  \item the loan, then the native pair — \textquotedblleft{}snēhita … geḷeya, geḷati\textquotedblright{}
  \item oil, then affection — \textquotedblleft{}snēha: oil … snēha: love\textquotedblright{}
  \item family, then friend — \textquotedblleft{}kuṭumba … snēhita\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}he is my friend.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ivanu nanna snēhita}.) What did \emph{snēha} mean before it meant \textquotedblleft{}affection\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Oil, smoothness.}) Name Kannada's native word for a friend. (\emph{\textbf{\kn{ಗೆಳೆಯ}}} \emph{geḷeya}, or \emph{\textbf{\kn{ಗೆಳತಿ}}} \emph{geḷati} for a woman.) Is \emph{kuṭumba} the people you choose, or the people you're born into? (\textbf{Born into} — \emph{snēhita} is who you choose.)
\end{tcolorbox}
